verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Gwalior engineering units with confirmed order books and bank-guarantee-backed EPC work; avoid pure capex-led capacity builders until MP GST turns positive.
title: Gwalior Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Gwalior engineering unit buys steel, castings and bought-out components, fabricates or machines them, and sells against purchase orders — so cash is tied up in the order book long before it returns as receivables.** Value sits in the order book and in the bank guarantees that win it, not in the shop floor [9]. Pricing power is thin: peers show volume growth without margin — Suzlon grew revenue 26% YoY to Rs 4,869 crore in Q2 FY27 while EBITDA stayed flat at Rs 720 crore and margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7]. **So when a proposal lands, check the order book and the margin trend together; if revenue is rising but EBITDA is flat, ask what price was conceded to win the order.**

## Where the cash actually sits
**The working-capital cycle is the whole credit story here — receivables and inventory net of payables, and for EPC work the cash conversion cycle runs longer than for OEMs [11].** Peers show what execution can do when the cycle is funded: DEE's revenue rose 77% YoY to Rs 286.7 crore and operating profit to Rs 47.6 crore in Q3 FY26 [5]; Skipper reported its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% [6]. **So take the monthly receivables-and-inventory statement, not the annual audited one; if debtor days stretch beyond the sanctioned cycle, ask which buyer and what retention is being held.** Capex is the second drain — Pitti is commissioning a Hyderabad facility in phases through FY 2030 on order visibility [4], and CRISIL notes players are adding capex to lift utilisation [11]. **If a borrower proposes greenfield capex without a signed order book, ask for the customer letters before any term loan.**

## What has changed now
**The local signal is weak even as the national one is strong: Madhya Pradesh GST collections are -0.1% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, 6.2 pp slower [D].** Nationally, IIP NIC 28 output is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date, and exports are +19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. **So treat the national numbers as the demand backdrop and the state GST as the local cash reality; if a Gwalior borrower's sales are growing faster than MP GST, ask where the goods are actually billed from.** Local news is thin on this industry: the only Gwalior-specific item is a GE Gwalior LT cable conversion tender [1], and the investment news is 12 multinationals and 24 telecom and textile proposals — interest, not yet plants, with investment size and timelines still unconfirmed [3]. The carpet story [2] is a different industry and does not inform this call.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue tier-2 fabricators and machining shops feeding transmission, railway and data-centre demand, and EPC subcontractors with bank-guarantee-backed orders [9][4].** Avoid pure capacity builders and single-customer units. **Structure every limit against the order book: take monthly stock and receivable statements, quarterly GST returns, and a half-yearly bank-guarantee utilisation report; if BG limits are exhausted relative to the order book, ask for the next order before enhancing.**

## Early-warning signs
- **GST turnover falling below the sanctioned projection for two quarters (monthly) -> freeze enhancement and re-price the limit.**
- **Debtor days rising while sales are flat (monthly) -> ask for the buyer-wise ageing and any retention money held.**
- **EBITDA margin slipping while revenue grows, as at Suzlon [7] (quarterly) -> cut the limit to the confirmed order book.**
- **BG invocation or a bid lost on pricing (event-based) -> collect from customer the reason and re-assess the pipeline.**

Margin slipping while revenue grows -> cut limit to confirmed order book
BG limits exhausted against order book -> ask for next order before enhancing
